title: Date centres should be built in planned precincts, inquiry finds
full_text:
Smarter planning controls encouraging artificial intelligence companies to develop in special precincts would avoid unwanted US-style data centre clusters in Sydney's densely populated suburbs, a parliamentary inquiry has found.
The committee found that in Sydney, data centre clusters are being built in areas like Lane Cove and Ryde simply because AI companies driven by market forces have found the capacity happens to exist there, not because of effective planning.
The state should instead plan for large-scale data centre development in precincts, supported by shared energy and water infrastructure, rather than as isolated developments, the inquiry found.
Lane Cove has become a suburban battleground between AI companies and angry locals, after a cluster of data centres began opening in industrial-zoned parts of the suburb. Community backlash led to data centre proponent Goodman to abandon their $1.2 billion proposal. Now locals in other parts of the state are looking to launch similar campaigns.
Among the 23 recommendations was a request that the government change planning requirements to place a greater emphasis on assessing the cumulative impacts of data centres, and to require AI companies to properly listen and respond to community concerns.
The inquiry also found the state government took an "entirely backwards" approach to data centre planning by opening up fast-track processes, including through the Investment Delivery Authority, but didn't release data centre guidelines until a year later.
That authority has endorsed at least 15 data centre projects in NSW valued at $51.89 billion, and the state has more than 60 data centres already operating or under construction.
Committee chair and Greens MP Abigail Boyd said fast-track processes like the Investment Delivery Authority, which she dubs the "tech bro concierge service", are leading to growing anguish in communities concerned about data centres popping up in their backyards.
She pointed to this week's midterm election results in the US, where anti-data-centre Democrats swept gubernatorial races.
"Unless we want to be where America is now, if we want to have actual sensible investment in data centres we need to slow down, pause those approvals and give the community time to breathe," she said.
"If we don't actually do what we've recommended in our report we will end up with people just getting angrier and angrier."
The state government recently removed council powers to automatically trigger a referral to the independent planning commission when they object to a state significant data centre, and increased the number of public objections needed to trigger a referral from 50 to 100.
